Subject: Unexplained trial credits across multiple Helio accounts

Hi Redwood team,

We just noticed an unusual cluster of trial credits that were automatically added to several Helio Labs signups this morning. The accounts look like they originated from our domain (heliolabs.ai) but with slight variations and disposable addresses (e.g., anna+test@heliolabs.ai, anna.test@heliolabs.ai). Quick triage notes (first pass):
- I pulled the grant events for the 12 account identifiers in Anna’s CSV. All were issued via the self-serve promo pipeline between 08:55–09:07 PDT this morning.
- Signals: 9/12 accounts have disposable-style local parts, 7/12 share the same device fingerprint hash (DFP: b1f7c9), and 5/12 share a narrow IP range that resolves to a cloud provider ASN.
- No existing paid activity on any of the accounts.

Recommended immediate actions:
1) Temporarily revoke the auto-issued credits on the 12 accounts and mark them as "suspicious" (prevents further consumption).
2) Suspend auto-crediting for new signups that match Helio domain variants or the device fingerprint for 48 hours while we investigate.
3) Provide Helio with the grant audit (CSV attached) and a brief timeline.

I attached a CSV with event IDs, timestamps, IPs, and UA strings (signup_signals_heliolabs.csv).

If Priyom can confirm this looks like an orchestrated abuse pattern, we should coordinate communications back to Helio and decide whether to permanently block these signups.

-Marissa

I completed a deeper signals analysis and payload correlation. Key findings:
- Device fingerprint b1f7c9 appears across ~18 accounts in the last 36 hours; UA strings show scripted headless Chromium variations.
- IP addresses resolve to two discreet subnets in a known proxy provider; reverse DNS shows rotating hostnames (proxy-*.net).
- The email local-part variants look intentionally obfuscated to bypass simple domain checks (plus-addressing mixed with dots).
- The self-serve grant pipeline used the default risk threshold; these requests were under burst volume (acceleration window) and bypassed extra validation due to a recent performance tweak to the grant flow (we lowered the behavioral hold timer).

Action recommendations:
1) Revoke credits for confirmed bot cluster accounts and mark as prevented from claiming future self-serve grants.
2) Revert the performance tweak immediately and re-enable the behavioral hold (adds 30s delay with bot-challenge if signals look anomalous).
3) Add device-fingerprint and proxy ASN to temporary deny-list for 72 hours while we complete the audit.
4) Prepare an audit package for Helio with grant events, IP traces, and the user-visible timeline.

I’ve created internal case FR-8421 and will drop detailed logs there: https://redwood.app/cases/FR-8421.

If Helio wants a formal post-mortem and a signed attestation we can schedule that with the security team.

-Priyom
Priyom Das
Fraud & Risk Engineering
Redwood Inference

What we found: automated test signups matched across disposable email variants, a common device fingerprint, and proxy-hosted IP ranges. The credit grants were processed by our self-serve pipeline during a short performance window; the lowered behavioral hold allowed these high-volume requests to pass initial checks.

Immediate actions we are taking (already in progress):
- Revoked credits on the 12 suspect accounts and marked them as suspended from consuming credits.
- Reverted the grant pipeline performance tweak and re-enabled the behavioral hold.
- Added the identified proxy ASN and the device fingerprint to a temporary deny-list for 72 hours.
- Created internal case FR-8421 with full logs and will produce a Helio-facing audit package by EOD tomorrow. Link: https://redwood.app/cases/FR-8421

We can also provide a signed attestation and the complete grant audit for your security team. Do you want us to temporarily hold any Helio-originating signups while we finish the audit, or would you prefer we only act on the suspicious accounts we already flagged?
